answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1928–1987 · American Pop artist, filmmaker and co-founder of Interview magazine
answer.sourceLine: Widely and consistently credited to Warhol, and entirely of a piece with his documented appetite for publicity — but no book, interview, letter or recording has been found that carries this wording. The earliest citation we could confirm is a Financial Times feature dated 5–6 December 2009, which itself quotes him without giving a source.

source.excerpt: Don’t pay any attention to what they write about you. Just measure it in inches.
trail: Quote Investigator has never taken this one up, and it is absent from Wikiquote’s Andy Warhol entry ↗ altogether — not in the sourced sections, not in the undated ones. We checked the page’s raw text: the words “inches,” “measure,” “weigh” and “clipping” do not occur anywhere in it, including the long run of quotations the entry draws from The Philosophy of Andy Warhol.

The aggregators carry it and cite nothing. Goodreads ↗ gives the exact wording under Warhol’s name with no book, no page and no year, beneath its own standing notice that “Quotes are added by the Goodreads community and are not verified by Goodreads.”

The oldest citation we could actually confirm is 2009, and it is second-hand. A 2010 post at A Boat Against the Current ↗ quotes the line and sources it to Jackie Wullschlager, “Triumph of the Ordinary,” Financial Times, 5–6 December 2009. That is a serious art critic repeating it — but a critic quoting Warhol in a feature is not a primary source, and she is not shown citing one.

A sibling version is openly doubted by the people who use it. Writing in 2014 about the variant “Don’t read your reviews, weigh them,” one blogger noted ↗ that it “is often attributed to Andy Warhol, but as with anything coming out of The Factory, it is, at the very best, a mere guess as to what the exact words were, if it was ever said at all,” citing Victor Bockris, Warhol: The Biography (Da Capo, 2003), p. 175, where the remark is mentioned in connection with Nick Rhodes of Duran Duran.
source.excerptNote: There is no fuller original context to show. Unlike Warhol’s documented remarks — the 1963 interview for “What Is Pop Art?”, the 1981 BBC Radio 3 conversation with Edward Lucie-Smith, the 1985 interview with Benjamin Buchloh, all of which Wikiquote reproduces with citations — this sentence arrives already free-floating, with no surrounding paragraph, no interviewer and no date.
source.rightsNote: We cannot assert a rights status, because we cannot identify the work. Nothing has been tied to a specific book, article, broadcast or recording, so there is no first-publication date to reason from — and Warhol’s own published books (The Philosophy of Andy Warhol, 1975; POPism, 1980) would in any case be firmly in copyright. Treat the sentence as unsourced text of unknown status rather than as public domain.

author.name: Andy Warhol
author.heading: Who Warhol was
author.metaLine: 1928–1987 · American Pop artist, filmmaker and co-founder of Interview magazine
author.bio: Andy Warhol was born in Pittsburgh on 6 August 1928 and died in New York on 22 February 1987. He spent the 1950s as a successful commercial illustrator before turning to fine art in the early 1960s, where the Campbell’s Soup Cans and the silkscreen portraits of Marilyn Monroe and Elvis Presley made him the most recognisable figure in Pop art. He also made films, ran the Factory, and in 1969 co-founded Interview — a magazine built entirely around the celebrity conversation, which is part of why a wisecrack about measuring your own press attaches to him so easily.

misattribution.heading: What gets claimed — and what holds up
misattribution.intro: This is not a case of the wrong name on the right sentence. It is the more common failure mode for a magnet name like Warhol’s: a line that everybody credits and nobody cites. Here are the claims we tested.

items.who: The Philosophy of Andy Warhol: From A to B and Back Again
items.why: Quote sites shelve the line beside Warhol’s best-known book because that is the title printed under his name on their author pages — not because anyone has pointed to a page in it. The Goodreads entry itself carries no citation ↗, and Wikiquote’s chapter-by-chapter selection from that book ↗ does not include it.

The same thought circulates in shorter forms — “weigh them,” “don’t read your press clippings, weigh them” — all credited to Warhol, none sourced. A 2014 post using that version ↗ concedes it is “at the very best, a mere guess as to what the exact words were, if it was ever said at all,” pointing to Bockris’s biography (2003, p. 175). When a saying has three interchangeable wordings and no fixed source, the wording is not evidence of anything.

This is the oldest appearance we could confirm, via a 2010 blog post that reproduces the citation ↗. It postdates Warhol’s death and quotes him without a source of its own, so it establishes circulation, not origin. We make no claim that nothing earlier exists — only that we did not find it.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer: Warhol may well have said this, and it sounds exactly like him — but as of this check nobody has produced the page, the tape or the interview. Until someone does, treat it as attributed, not documented. Compare it with the Warhol remarks that are sourced ↗, each of which comes with a publication, an interviewer or a date.

context.heading: Why the line sticks
lead: “Inches” is newsroom shorthand: column inches, the vertical space a story takes up on the page. The joke is that press coverage should be handled the way an advertiser handles it — as area purchased rather than as opinion received. Whether the write-up is admiring or savage is beside the point; what counts is how much of the page you occupied.

That is a very Warhol proposition, which is exactly why the attribution is so frictionless. He built a career on the mechanics of publicity: he moved from 1950s commercial illustration into silkscreen portraits of Marilyn Monroe and Elvis Presley, and in 1969 he co-founded Interview, a magazine devoted to the celebrity Q&A, as The Andy Warhol Museum’s account of his life ↗ sets out. A line about measuring your own press is so plausible in his mouth that nobody stops to ask where it came from — and that is precisely the condition under which unsourced quotations survive.
context.detailsSummary: Why this page says “attributed” and not something firmer
detailsBody: Why “attributed” rather than “disputed”: we found no rival originator, no earlier claimant, and no evidence that the sentence was invented and pinned on Warhol. What we found was silence — no primary source in either direction. Absence of a citation is a reason to hedge, not a reason to convict.

Why not “verified”: Warhol’s recorded talk is unusually well preserved — taped interviews, two ghost-assisted memoirs, a posthumously published diary — so a genuine Warhol aphorism usually has a findable home. This one does not. If you can point to the book, broadcast or transcript, we will upgrade the page and credit you.
context.pull: Everyone quotes it. Nobody cites it.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's Andy Warhol entry does not contain this quote, nor any variant using the words 'inches', 'measure', 'weigh' or 'clipping' — including its extensive section of quotations from The Philosophy of Andy Warhol (1975), and its sourced 1963, 1981 (BBC Radio 3, Edward Lucie-Smith) and 1985 (Benjamin Buchloh) interview sections.

Goodreads carries the exact wording 'Don't pay any attention to what they write about you. Just measure it in inches.' credited to Andy Warhol with no source cited, under a notice reading 'Quotes are added by the Goodreads community and are not verified by Goodreads.'

A 2010 blog post gives the quote as Andy Warhol's and sources it to Jackie Wullschlager, 'Triumph of the Ordinary: Shaped by the Depression, Andy Warhol Created an Art of Transfiguration and Plenty', The Financial Times, December 5-6, 2009.

A 17 November 2014 post states that 'Don't read your reviews, weigh them' is often attributed to Andy Warhol but 'as with anything coming out of The Factory, it is, at the very best, a mere guess as to what the exact words were, if it was ever said at all', and cites Bockris, 2003: 175 (Victor Bockris, Warhol: The Biography, Da Capo Press) as mentioning the quote in relation to Nick Rhodes of Duran Duran.

Wikipedia gives Andy Warhol's birth date as August 6, 1928 (Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania) and death as February 22, 1987, describes him as an American artist and filmmaker and leading figure in Pop art, and lists his books The Philosophy of Andy Warhol (1975), POPism (1980) and The Andy Warhol Diaries (1989).

The Andy Warhol Museum's life page gives born August 6, 1928 and died February 22, 1987, describes his 1950s commercial-illustration career, his 1962 Campbell's Soup Cans and celebrity portraits of Marilyn Monroe and Elvis Presley, and states he co-founded Interview magazine in 1969.
The Internet Archive holds a borrowable scan of 'The philosophy of Andy Warhol: from A to B and back again' by Andy Warhol (1928-1987), published by Harcourt, New York.
The Internet Archive holds a borrowable scan of 'POPism: the Warhol 60s' by Andy Warhol with Pat Hackett, Harcourt Brace Jovanovich, New York, 1980.
